q-126574.name: Question 1
q-126574.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the vector field $F(x,y)?$

I. $F(x,y)=⟨y{e}^{x},\,x-{e}^{x}⟩$

II. $F(x,y)=⟨2y,\,x⟩$

III. $F(x,y)=⟨-\frac{y}{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2},\,\frac{2x}{3}+1⟩$
q-126574.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if $F(x,y)=⟨P(x,y),\,Q(x,y)⟩,$ where

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field I does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{x}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1-{e}^{x},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-2{e}^{x}\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field II does *not* give the required area. Notice that 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field III gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{3}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{2}{3},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
q-42301.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos⁡t−cos⁡2t,sin⁡t−sin⁡2t⟩ for t∈[π3,5π3]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫π/35π/3AAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
b
(cos⁡t−cos⁡2t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
c
(cos⁡2t−cos⁡t)(cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t)
d
(sin⁡2t−sin⁡t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
e
(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t,cos⁡t−2cos⁡2t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫π/35π/3−(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)⋅(−sin⁡t+2sin⁡2t)dt=∫π/35π/3(sin⁡t−sin⁡2t)(sin⁡t−2sin⁡2t)dt.

q-42315.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/bfec7cbdb26a3db773ab1f6207de436ff0856b331cda183da530dbb6b91d91bd.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{cos}^{3}⁡t,\,{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
q-42315.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos3⁡t,sin3⁡t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3sin3⁡tcos3⁡t
b
3sin3⁡tcos4⁡t
c
3sin2⁡tcos4⁡t
d
3sin3⁡tcos2⁡t
e
3sin4⁡tcos2⁡t
Submit

EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=0−(−1)=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=−y and Q(x,y)=0, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮C−ydx.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t,3sin2⁡tcos⁡t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮C−ydx=∫02π(−sin3⁡t)⋅(−3cos2⁡tsin⁡t)dt=∫02π3sin4⁡tcos2⁡tdt.

q-42297.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/35b8ad6fd40daf95ba4f77288321d6a570e2df2944d056b9445e9ba4e36f97b7.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
q-42297.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Let D be the region enclosed by the curve C parametrized as r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t,3sin⁡t−sin⁡3t⟩ for t∈[0,2π]. The area of D can be written as

Area(D)=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∫02πAAAAAAAdt,

where P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x. Determine the missing part of the equation.

a
3(3cos⁡t+cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
b
−3(sin⁡t+sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
c
3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)
d
−3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
e
3(sin⁡t−sin⁡3t)(3sin⁡t−3sin⁡3t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path C is positively oriented, and

∂Q∂x−∂P∂y=1−0=1.

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region D enclosed by the curve C as follows:

Area(D)=∬DdA=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∮CPdx+Qdy

Substituting P(x,y)=0 and Q(x,y)=x, we get

∮CPdx+Qdy=∮Cxdy.

The derivative of r(t) is r′(t)=⟨−3sin⁡t+3sin⁡3t,3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t⟩.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

∮Cxdy=∫02π(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)⋅(3cos⁡t−3cos⁡3t)dt=∫02π3(3cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)(cos⁡t−cos⁡3t)dt.

q-126761.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247150/assets/10f4094edb09afc7908bd0cd3df089387c8f5b762ea5ef86da152d1c9d08b5e4.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{sin}^{5}⁡t,\,{cos}^{5}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*
q-126761.worked_solution:
Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨5{sin}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{sin}^{5}⁡t)\cdot (-5{cos}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5{sin}^{6}⁡t{cos}^{4}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
